docs.title: Jean-Michel
docs.text:
An opinionated AI assistant for rigorous, constrained, asynchronous software development.

Jean-Michel orchestrates background engineering work with clear scope boundaries, isolated worktrees, and reviewable commits.

docs.title: Architecture Overview
docs.text:
Jean-Michel is composed of five major layers:

Developer(s)
      ↓
Conversation Timeline (single persistent channel)
      ↓
Primary Agent (semantic interpreter)
      ↓
Scheduler / Orchestrator
      ↓
Execution Bricks (code, tests, commits, analysis, coverage, etc.)

The developer is not chatting with an LLM session. They interact with a persistent project-level entity that reads timeline intent and schedules execution.

docs.title: Scheduler and Orchestration Engine
docs.text:
The scheduler:

  • reads the conversation timeline
  • decides whether to respond
  • creates task graphs
  • manages worktrees
  • supervises commit production
  • selectively integrates branches

Task execution may rely on a Dask-based scheduler (via Curry or equivalent), allowing:

  • dependency graphs
  • parallel task execution
  • deterministic chaining
  • post-task hooks (for example continuous analysis)

docs.title: Worktree Model
docs.text:
Every feature or improvement:

  • spawns a dedicated Git worktree
  • creates isolated branches
  • produces structured commits
  • runs lint/hooks/tests
  • reports status to the scheduler

No background mutation touches main directly.

docs.title: Execution Bricks
docs.text:
Reusable bricks include:

  • code generation
  • AST mutation
  • refactoring
  • test writing and execution
  • coverage analysis
  • commit creation
  • linting/pre-commit
  • monitoring

docs.title: Monitoring and Dashboard
docs.text:
For each branch, Jean-Michel tracks:

  • diff size
  • files added/deleted/modified
  • commit count
  • coverage delta
  • structural impact

Branches are scored by cognitive load (green/orange/red) to prioritize review.

docs.title: What "Asynchronous" Means
docs.text:
Interaction and execution are decoupled.

You continuously interact with one persistent agent without waiting for previous tasks to finish. Messages are translated into background tasks.

There is:

  • one interface
  • one timeline
  • one persistent agent
  • no session resets
  • no parallel chat threads

docs.title: Philosophy
docs.text:
Jean-Michel is built around four principles:

  1. Constraint-first engineering.
  2. Autonomy without opacity.
  3. Worktree isolation.
  4. Merge-ready output.

docs.title: Commitology
docs.text:
Commitology enforces disciplined commit production.

It includes:

  • conventional commit adherence
  • style inference from repository history
  • structured commit generation
  • Commitizen integration when available

docs.title: AST-Based Structural Editing (optional)
docs.text:
Instead of raw text edits, Jean-Michel can:

  • parse Python into AST
  • modify structural nodes
  • regenerate normalized code

docs.title: Initialization Layer
docs.text:
On first integration with a project, Jean-Michel creates and versions .jean-michel/ metadata for:

  • features
  • constraints
  • scope rules
  • historical commit analysis
  • monitoring metadata

docs.title: Features and Constraints
docs.text:
Jean-Michel distinguishes:

  • constraints: negative scopes / hard exclusions
  • features: positive authorized scopes

Rules:

  • constraints override features
  • scope conflicts are detected
  • conflicts are surfaced in monitoring/dashboard

docs.title: Continuous Analysis
docs.text:
Jean-Michel can continuously monitor:

  • duplication
  • imports
  • dead code
  • bad practices
  • refactor opportunities
  • coverage regressions

It can propose improvement branches and follow-up tasks.

docs.title: Multi-Device Continuity
docs.text:
Jean-Michel is repository-centric, not machine-centric.

A background sync task can:

  • fetch remote updates
  • detect new commits/branch movement
  • evaluate sync state
  • trigger analysis on remote changes

Git remains the source of truth for repository history.

docs.title: Feature-Aware Evolution
docs.text:
Features are treated as scoped, versioned engineering units.

The scheduler can reason about cross-feature interactions and classify conflicts such as:

  • scope overlap
  • contract violations
  • coverage regressions
  • responsibility drift
  • hidden coupling

Constraint rules remain dominant over feature scopes.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text: Jean-Michel is intended to be installed and used from another repository.

docs.title: Option 1: Install from PyPI
docs.text:
From your target project root:

uv add jean-michel

Then use the CLI:

uv run jm --help

docs.title: Option 2: Install from a Local Path (development phase)
docs.text:
If you are iterating locally on Jean-Michel and want to consume it from another repo:

uv add --editable /absolute/path/to/jean-michel

Then:

uv run jm --help

docs.title: Conversation DB Path
docs.text:
Jean-Michel stores conversation data in DuckDB.

You can force a specific database path with:

JEAN_MICHEL_DB_PATH=/path/to/your/project/.jean-michel/storage.duckdb uv run jm lm

If this variable is not set, the default path is:

.jean-michel/storage.duckdb

docs.title: API Port Strategy
docs.text:
By default, Jean-Michel computes a deterministic API port per repository (range 5600-6599) from repository identity. This avoids port collisions when multiple repositories use Jean-Michel on the same machine.

To force a specific port:

JEAN_MICHEL_API_PORT=5656 make api

docs.title: Coverage Command
docs.text:
Coverage is computed in an isolated worktree at the selected commit.

Default command:

uv run pytest --cov --cov-report=xml

Override command when needed:

JEAN_MICHEL_COVERAGE_CMD="uv run pytest --cov --cov-report=xml --cov=your_package" uv run jm api

You can also update the command at runtime from:

  • Repository tab in the web app
  • API endpoints: GET /api/coverage/command, POST /api/coverage/command
  • MCP tools: get_coverage_command, set_coverage_command

docs.title: MCP + VSCode Setup
docs.text: This guide explains how to connect VSCode to the Jean-Michel MCP server.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• jean-michel installed in your target project (PyPI or editable)
  • uv available on your machine
  • VSCode MCP support enabled

docs.title: 1. Open MCP Servers in VSCode
docs.text: Open the MCP server picker in VSCode.

docs.title: 2. Add a new MCP server
docs.text: Click Add MCP Server.

docs.title: 3. Choose Command (stdio)
docs.text: Pick Command (stdio).

docs.title: 4. Enter the command
docs.text:
Use this command:

uv run jm mcp --transport stdio

If prompted for command/args separately:

  • Command: uv
  • Args: run jm mcp --transport stdio

docs.title: 5. Save in workspace settings
docs.text: Use workspace-level config if you want this server only for the current repository.

docs.title: Recommended values
docs.text:
• Working directory: your project root where jean-michel is installed
  • Example: /path/to/your/project
  • Optional environment:
  • JEAN_MICHEL_DB_PATH=/path/to/your/project/.jean-michel/storage.duckdb

JEAN_MICHEL_DB_PATH defines the exact DuckDB file used by Jean-Michel. If omitted, Jean-Michel uses the default repository-local path:

.jean-michel/storage.duckdb

docs.title: Verify it works
docs.text:
Once connected, your assistant should see these MCP tools:

  • list_messages
  • send_message
  • get_default_actor

docs.title: Optional: HTTP mode
docs.text:
If you prefer an HTTP MCP server:

uv run jm mcp --transport streamable-http --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8001

Then add an HTTP MCP server in VSCode with URL:

http://127.0.0.1:8001/mcp
